titleText.es: Ya nos divorciamos una vez por el asunto del avión sobre una cinta transportadora. (Respuesta preventiva a los inevitables hilos que van a discutir sobre el tema: estáis todos equivocados en internet).
titleText.en: We actually divorced once over the airplane/treadmill argument.  (Preemptive response to the inevitable threads arguing about it:  you're all wrong on the internet.)
titleText.noteEn: The English text is the official xkcd title text, including its two spaces before the parenthesis and after the colon. The Spanish archive renders the treadmill as una cinta transportadora and uses the Spain form estáis todos equivocados.

regions.labelEs: ME ECHÓ DE CASA GRITANDO: "NO PRONUNCIES ESAS PALABRAS". "NO EN ESTA CASA".

applications.explanationEn: Me identifies the person forced out, echó is the completed-past action, and de casa names the place that person had to leave.
The accented completed-past form echó presents the expulsion as one finished event.
Gritando uses the -ando form to show the action happening at the same time as the expulsion.
No comes first, and ordinary pronuncias changes to the negative-command form pronuncies for one familiar person.

regions.labelEs: HAN PASADO DOS AÑOS. PENSÉ QUE LAS HERIDAS ESTARÍAN CURADAS.

applications.explanationEn: Han is the helper for a plural subject, and pasado is the completed-action form that carries the elapsed-time meaning.
Pensé presents the thought as a completed event in the past.

applications.exampleEs: PENSÉ QUE LAS HERIDAS ESTARÍAN CURADAS
applications.explanationEn: Pensé fixes the viewpoint in the past, que introduces the complete thought about las heridas, and estarían places their state later than that thought.
Estarían keeps the full form estar and adds the plural conditional ending -ían.
Estarían supplies the state helper, while curadas is the feminine plural completed-action form matching heridas.
Lo que introduces an unnamed thing or idea—the content that was previously said.
Dije presents the act of saying as a completed past event.

regions.labelEs: PLUTÓN NUNCA TUVO QUE HABER SIDO UN PLANETA.

applications.explanationEn: Tuvo que supplies completed-past necessity, and the filled action slot is the full unchanged perfect form haber sido.
Tuvo presents the past necessity as a completed instance rather than ongoing background.
Haber stays unchanged after the earlier verb, and sido is the completed-action form of ser.

Nunca negates the retrospective necessity built with tuvo que haber sido. In this translated line it rejects the earlier classification; a more direct Spanish way to express the official source's “should never have been” is nunca debió haber sido.

cards.promptEs: echar a alguien de un lugar
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is forced to leave a place?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of echar for forcing the person out, then de before the place being left.
cards.noteEn: The person can follow echar with personal a: echaron a Leo del aula. A short object word instead goes before a changed form of echar: lo echaron del aula, me echó de casa. De introduces the place the person is forced to leave.

example.es: La directora lo echó del aula.
example.en: The principal threw him out of the classroom.

cards.noteEn: Echó is a completed-past form of echar. With a person and de plus a place, echar means forcing that person to leave the place.

example.es: El casero lo echó del piso.
example.en: The landlord threw him out of the apartment.

cards.answerEn: Use the preterite for a completed event and the imperfect for background, an ongoing situation, or something that used to happen.
cards.noteEn: Think of a story: the preterite answers “What happened next?” The imperfect answers “What was happening?”, “What were things like?”, or “What used to happen?” These two names describe how the speaker presents an event, not simply how long it lasted.
cards.questionEn: Spanish has two common ways to talk about the past. When do you use each one?

example.en: While I was walking, it started to rain.

cards.noteEn: After echar in the sense of forcing someone to leave, de introduces the place the person must leave.

example.en: They threw him out of the office.

cards.noteEn: Gritando is the ongoing-action form of gritar. When it appears on its own after another action, it can add how that action was happening.

cards.promptEs: -ando / -iendo para una acción simultánea o un medio
cards.questionEn: How can you add an action that happens at the same time or explains how something is done?
cards.answerEn: Use the action form ending in -ando or -iendo, such as hablando or corriendo.
cards.noteEn: Spanish calls this form the gerund. It does not change for the person. Used on its own, it can describe a simultaneous action or the means used: Entró corriendo means the person entered by running. This differs from estar plus the same form, which focuses on an action in progress.

cards.promptEs: orden negativa de tú: no + verbo
cards.questionEn: How do you tell one friend or familiar person not to do something?
cards.answerEn: Put no before the verb's special negative-command form. If the verb uses te, put te between no and the verb.
cards.noteEn: For a regular -ar verb, the negative form usually ends in -es: hablar becomes no hables. Regular -er and -ir verbs usually end in -as: comer becomes no comas. A short word such as te goes before this negative form, as in no te levantes.

cards.answerEn: say; utter (negative command to one familiar person)
cards.noteEn: For an ordinary statement to tú, pronunciar gives pronuncias. After no in a negative command to that same person, the ending changes to pronuncies.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: Pasado is the completed-action form of pasar. With a form of haber and a duration, it says that an amount of time has gone by.
Años is the plural of año. Keep the ñ: anos without it is a different word.

example.en: We lived there for two years.

cards.noteEn: Pensé is the completed-past form of pensar for the speaker. Before que, it introduces what the speaker thought.

example.en: I thought you were arriving tomorrow.

cards.promptEs: verbo o contexto en pasado + que/cuándo/etc. + forma en -ría
cards.questionEn: How do you report that something was still in the future at an earlier point in time?
cards.answerEn: Set the reporting viewpoint in the past, introduce the reported statement or question, and put the later action or state in a Spanish 'would' form.
cards.noteEn: A past verb, or surrounding words that clearly place the report in the past, establishes the earlier viewpoint. Que can introduce a reported statement, while an accented question word such as cuándo or dónde can introduce an embedded question. The later verb uses the conditional—the form usually made by keeping its dictionary form and adding -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, or -ían—to show what would happen or be true after that past point.

example.es: Lucía dijo que llegaría el lunes.
example.en: Lucía said she would arrive on Monday.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.noteEn: Estarían keeps the full dictionary form estar and adds -ían. It can describe the later state of several people or things from a past point of view.

example.en: I thought they would be ready.

cards.questionEn: How do you form a Spanish “would” verb such as “would forget”?
cards.answerEn: Keep the whole dictionary form and add a conditional ending such as -ía.
cards.noteEn: The same endings attach to verbs ending in -ar, -er, and -ir. The ending changes for the person: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, or -ían.

cards.promptEs: estar + forma de acción completada que describe un estado
cards.questionEn: How do you describe the state something is in as the result of an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by the action's completed form, with an ending that matches the thing being described.
cards.noteEn: The completed form, often ending in -ado or -ido, is also called a participle. Estar changes for who or what is in the state. The participle changes like a describing word: cerrado, cerrada, cerrados, or cerradas. This pattern focuses on the resulting state, not on who performed the action.
Curadas is the feminine plural completed-action form of curar when it describes the resulting state of feminine plural things.
Mantengo is the present form of mantener for the speaker. With a statement, opinion, or decision, it means continuing to support it rather than changing one's position.

example.en: I stand by what I wrote.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Lo combines with que to refer to an idea, action, or whole situation rather than a masculine noun. Together, lo que means “what” or “the thing that.”

cards.questionEn: How do you say “what” or “the thing that” without naming a specific object?
cards.answerEn: Use lo que to refer to an idea, action, situation, or unnamed thing.
cards.noteEn: Here lo is neutral: it does not stand for a masculine noun. Que introduces the information that identifies the idea or thing. Together they work as one unit.

example.en: I don't understand what you're saying.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Here que completes lo que, a neutral expression meaning “what” or “the thing that.” It does not refer to a particular masculine or feminine noun.
Dije is the completed-past form of decir for the speaker.
Spanish writes the astronomical name Plutón with an accent on the final syllable.

example.es: Plutón está más lejos del Sol que Neptuno.
example.en: Pluto is farther from the Sun than Neptune.

cards.answerEn: Pluto was classified as a dwarf planet rather than one of the Solar System's eight planets under the International Astronomical Union's 2006 definition.
cards.noteEn: The 2006 definition requires a Solar System planet to orbit the Sun, be nearly round, and have cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit. Pluto meets the first two conditions but not the third, so the IAU placed it in the distinct dwarf-planet category.
Tuvo is a completed-past form of tener. Before que and an unchanged action verb, it forms a past version of tener que, meaning that something was necessary or required.

cards.promptEs: tener que + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone has to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of tener, then que, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Only tener changes for the person and time: tengo que, tienes que, tiene que, and so on. The final action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes tener que, “to have to”

cards.noteEn: After a verb such as debería, haber remains in its dictionary form and combines with a completed-action form such as llamado or comido. In this construction, haber is a helper rather than the hay construction meaning “there is.”

cards.questionEn: How do you refer to an action that was already completed after another verb such as poder, deber, or parecer?
cards.answerEn: Use the unchanged helper haber followed by the completed-action form of the main verb.
cards.noteEn: The completed-action form is often called a participle: terminar becomes terminado, hacer becomes hecho, and ser becomes sido. After another verb, haber stays unchanged. The plus sign in the prompt means “followed by.”
Sido is the completed-action form of ser. It follows a form of haber: ha sido means “has been,” and haber sido means “to have been.”
